scene.bubble: Zoom out! See why mending matters for the planet, learn relative clauses, and master the gapped text.
scene.intro: Welcome to Unit 4. The Inspiring Nordic project looks at the bigger picture: what our throwaway habits do to the environment, and why the trades are part of the answer. In this unit you read a documentary-style article on sustainability, you learn relative clauses to add information smoothly, and you practise the gapped-text task from Reading and Use of English Part 6. Can repairing help save the planet? Let's see.

data.title: Why mending matters
data.author: sofia
data.text:
For Inspiring Nordic, we researched a question that felt huge: what happens to all the things we throw away? The answer, which shocked us, is that most of them end up in a landfill or are burned, releasing gases that warm the planet.

Every year the world produces millions of tonnes of waste, much of which could be avoided. A chair that is broken is usually replaced, not repaired. Yet the trades we have been studying — carpenters, tailors and electricians, whose skills keep objects alive — offer a quiet solution.

Sofía, who led our research, discovered a local workshop where old furniture is restored instead of dumped. Mateo, whose grandfather was a shoemaker, reminded us that mending was once completely normal.

The idea is simple. Products that are built to last, and craftspeople who can repair them, reduce the waste that damages our environment. A jacket repaired is a jacket that never reaches the landfill.

Nadia summed it up: “The most sustainable object is the one you already own.” Seen this way, the humble trades — which many people ignore — are part of the bigger picture. Every repaired item is a small victory for the planet, and a reason to value the people who make things last.

activities.title: Grammar — Relative clauses (defining, non-defining and reduced)

data.title: Relative clauses (defining, non-defining and reduced)
data.intro: Relative clauses give more information about a noun. Defining clauses identify which one we mean; non-defining clauses (with commas) add extra information; reduced clauses leave out the relative pronoun and the auxiliary.

examples.text: The workshop that restores furniture is near school.
Sofía, who led our research, found the workshop.
Mateo, whose grandfather was a shoemaker, agreed.
A jacket repaired never reaches the landfill.

rules: Defining clauses identify the noun and use who/which/that with no commas.
Non-defining clauses add extra information, use commas, and never use that.
You can reduce a clause by dropping who/which + be (the man who is waiting → the man waiting).

items.sentence: The tailor ___ repaired my coat is very skilled.
Nadia, ___ idea impressed us, spoke last.
That is the workshop ___ we visited last week.
My uncle, ___ lives in Lima, is a carpenter.
The items ___ in the bin could have been repaired.

activities.title: Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations

data.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first. Use the KEY WORD. Write between two and five words.

items.first: The workshop is near school. It restores old furniture.
Sofía found the workshop. She led our research.
Mateo told us about mending. His grandfather was a shoemaker.
The jacket was repaired, so it never reached the landfill.
We visited a workshop last week. It restores furniture.

activities.title: Use of English Part 2 — open cloze. Write ONE word in each gap.

data.text: Repairing an old object is often better than buying a new {1}. A chair {2} a broken leg can easily be mended. The people {3} do this work are skilled craftspeople. Their workshop, {4} we visited last week, was full {5} restored furniture. It is a habit {6} we should all develop.

data.voice_note: Voz: la profesora (Miss Vega), presentando el texto sobre el medio ambiente.
data.script: Good morning, Grade 10. Our reading today is about sustainability, which links directly to the trades project. Here is the key idea: every object we repair is one less object in the landfill. The Cambridge exam calls this task the gapped text, where you fit missing paragraphs into an article. Read carefully and follow the pronouns; a word like which or who often tells you what comes before. For Thursday, find one thing at home that could be repaired instead of replaced. Sofía will start our discussion. Small choices matter.

questions.q: Every object we repair is one less object in the …
The Cambridge task here is called the … text.

activities.title: Speaking — consumption and the planet. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, discuss consumption and the environment. Model: “The most sustainable jacket is the one that you already own.” 1) What is something you own that you could repair instead of replacing? 2) Why do you think people, who used to mend things, now throw them away? 3) Should schools teach basic repair skills, which many families have lost? Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Write a short opinion text (8–10 sentences) about reducing waste in your community. Use at least four relative clauses — defining, non-defining and one reduced (e.g. 'The workshop, which restores furniture, is popular' / 'items thrown away too soon'). Capital letters and full stops!
